title: Is the SIR Led by a Remote-Controlled Computer?
shows: Rajeev Kumar, a former professor of computer science at IIT Kharagpur, IIT Kanpur, BITS Pilani and JNU, argues that a roll of nearly a billion electors needs a computerised database and that the trouble with the revision lies in poor governance of the exercise. He sets out six weaknesses as he sees them. The rolls of 2002 to 2004, prepared largely on paper and digitised later, are used to map electors without being checked first. The rules for logical discrepancies are not public and reportedly grew from six categories to eleven. Reports allege bulk deletions with no identifiable applicant and inserted code that generated Form 7 objections, which he says need an independent inquiry. Reports of restricted access suggest registration officers could not verify, correct or restore records. He says a pilot should have tested the mapping, the rules and the forms before the exercise began, and the Commission declined in reply to an RTI request to describe the software that flags errors. He asks for a separate form or workflow to restore wrongly deleted names in place of Form 6, and for an independent technical audit of ECINet by industry experts, possibly led by Nandan Nilekani, and he says the academic review proposed in the Commission's press note of 26 September may not be enough.
quote: Security controls must not override statutory authority: EROs need authorised access to fulfil their legal responsibilities.
An academic review alone, as proposed in the ECI’s press note dated September 26, 2026, may be inadequate to establish the technical integrity and security of a system of this scale.
note: First reading, 9 November 2026. Read in full through The Wire's CMS API (posts/detail) with curl on 9 November 2026. Published 9 November 2026 at 11:40 am IST (post_date_gmt 06:10:34), byline Rajeev Kumar, whose line at the foot describes him as a former Professor of Computer Science at IIT Kharagpur, IIT Kanpur, BITS Pilani and JNU and a former scientist at DRDO and DST. The column carries two images, a lead illustration credited to Pariplab Chakraborty and The Wire's 'SIR: What Counts?' series image. The arguments are his own. Much of what he relies on is reported elsewhere on the site. The Azamgarh entries are up-23 and up-24, the suspension of two registration officers of Pilibhit is up-30, and the deactivation of computer assistants' ECINET logins in Uttar Pradesh is up-29, the e-signing of tribunal orders in West Bengal is soft-50, the separation of the declaration from the online Form 6 is soft-53, and the two Election Commissioners' objections are court-31. The Commission's press note of 26 September is on the reading list. He names no source for the RTI reply or for the growth of the discrepancy categories, and both are given as he reports them. His view that bulk deletions may attract penalties under section 32 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 is not carried.
